To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the stochasticity in viral dynamics in a spatially distributed population can lead to oscillations in viral load, even if the underlying deterministic model is monotonic; 2) the oscillations can arise even in the presence of a strong density dependence in the underlying dynamics; 3) the oscillations in viral loads can be observed in the absence of any oscillations in the population dynamics; 4) the oscillations are not a consequence of any particular spatial structure of the host population

(a) the stochasticity of viral dynamics in a spatially distributed population can lead to oscillations of viral abundance and (b) these oscillations can be explained by the interplay of the spatial distribution of the host population with the spatial distribution of viral particles.

the development and use of mathematical models for the study of the dynamics of infectious diseases in spatially structured populations, in particular, the role of stochasticity in the dynamics of epidemics in structured populations.
